hook.situation: Pointing out the exact item, place, food, book, or person you mean by putting a description before the noun.
objectives: Use A-ㄴ/은 N for adjective descriptions: 작은 가방, 조용한 카페.
Use V-는 N for present or habitual action descriptions: 손님이 찾는 모델, 제가 읽는 책.
Recognize completed action modifiers that appear in real shopping talk: 어제 본 가방, 새로 들어온 물건.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean descriptions come before the noun. Once learners can build 작은 가방 and 어제 본 가방, they can identify the right thing without making several short disconnected sentences.

grammarNotes.title: A-(으)ㄴ N — Adjectives describing a noun
grammarNotes.func: To put an adjective in front of a noun (a *pretty* bag, a *small* room), you can't use the plain dictionary form. You change the adjective into a modifying form with -(으)ㄴ and put it right before the noun.

formTable.when: Adjective stem ends in a vowel
Adjective stem ends in a consonant

examples.note: 예쁘다 ends in a vowel, so just add ㄴ → 예쁜, right before 가방.

examples.en: I live in a small house.
examples.note: 작다 ends in a consonant, so add 은 → 작은. The adjective goes straight onto the noun — no 이/가.

examples.en: I waited for a long time.
examples.note: 길다 is a ㄹ-stem: the ㄹ drops and ㄴ is added → 긴, not 길은.
맛있다/맛없다 act like verbs, so they take 는, not 은 → 맛있는.

keyPoint.label: 예쁜 가방 vs 가방이 예뻐요
keyPoint.body: Korean uses an adjective in two ways. Before a noun it has to become the modifier form (예쁜 가방 = 'a pretty bag'). At the end of a sentence it stays as the predicate (가방이 예뻐요 = 'The bag is pretty'). Same adjective, two jobs — don't put the plain 예뻐요 form in front of a noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 좋은 is said [조은] (joeun): the ㅎ drops out between vowels and the sound links straight into the next syllable. 작은 links the same way as [자근] (jageun).

drill.instruction: Turn the adjective in parentheses into the -(으)ㄴ modifier form and attach it to the noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English leaves the adjective unchanged ('an expensive bag'), so learners reach for the sentence form 비싸요. But before a noun a Korean adjective needs the modifier ending: 비싸다 → 비싼 가방. The polite 비싸요 can only close a sentence (가방이 비싸요).

grammarNotes.title: V-는 N — A present/habitual action describing a noun
grammarNotes.func: To describe a noun by an action happening now or done regularly (the person who is *eating*, the book I *read* these days), add -는 to the verb stem and put it before the noun. It works like an English 'who/that' clause ('the person who eats').

examples.en: The person eating is my friend.
examples.note: 먹다 + 는 → 먹는. The whole chunk '밥을 먹는' describes 사람, and the object 밥을 stays inside it.

examples.en: It's the school I go to often.
examples.note: 가다 is a vowel stem; -는 still attaches → 가는, and 자주 ('often') gives it the habitual meaning.

examples.en: He's a student who studies Korean.
examples.note: 공부하다 → 공부하는; -는 marks an ongoing/habitual action describing 학생.

examples.en: The book I'm reading now is fun.
examples.note: 읽다 + 는 → 읽는 [잉는]; 지금 ('now') makes the in-progress meaning clear.

keyPoint.label: 먹는 사람 vs 예쁜 사람
keyPoint.body: Verbs and adjectives use different modifier endings in the present. A verb (an action) takes -는: 먹는 사람 ('the person who eats'). An adjective (a state) takes -(으)ㄴ: 예쁜 사람 ('a pretty person'). Just ask 'is this a doing-word or a describing-word?' to pick the ending.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹는 is said [멍는] (meongneun): a ㄱ before ㄴ turns into an [ㅇ] sound (nasal assimilation). 읽는 → [잉는] (ingneun) the same way.

drill.instruction: Make the verb into the present V-는 modifier and attach it to the noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 먹은 사람 (for 'the person who is eating')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'eating' is one word, so learners mix up the endings. For an action happening now or regularly, use -는 (먹는 사람). Putting -(으)ㄴ on a verb (먹은) means a *finished* action ('the person who ate') — a different time.

grammarNotes.title: V-(으)ㄴ N — A finished (past) action describing a noun
grammarNotes.func: To describe a noun by an action that's already over (the movie I *saw* yesterday, the person who *came*), add -(으)ㄴ to the verb stem and put it before the noun. It marks the action as done — the past version of the 'who/that' clause.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
Verb stem ends in a consonant

examples.en: The movie I saw yesterday was good.
examples.note: 보다 is a vowel stem → 본; 어제 ('yesterday') shows it's finished, so we use -(으)ㄴ, not -는.

examples.en: The meal I ate earlier was delicious.
examples.note: 먹다 ends in a consonant → 먹은 [머근]; the meal is already eaten — a finished action.

examples.en: It's the food my friend made.
examples.note: 만들다 is a ㄹ-stem: drop the ㄹ, add ㄴ → 만든 (not 만들은).

examples.en: I'm listening again to the song I heard yesterday.
examples.note: 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before 은 → 들은 (not 듣은).

keyPoint.label: 본 영화 vs 보는 영화
keyPoint.body: On a verb, the ending sets the time. -(으)ㄴ = finished/past (어제 본 영화 = 'the movie I saw'). -는 = now or habitual (지금 보는 영화 = 'the movie I'm watching now'). Pick the ending by *when* the action happens compared to now.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 먹은 links as [머근] (meogeun) and 읽은 as [일근] (ilgeun): the final consonant slides into the next syllable. 만든 (from 만들다) is just [만든] (mandeun).

drill.instruction: Make the verb into the past V-(으)ㄴ modifier and attach it to the noun.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 어제 봤은 영화 / 어제 보는 영화 (for 'the movie I saw yesterday')
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners either glue the past -았/었- onto the modifier (봤은 ✗) or fall back on -는. Don't add -았/었- before the noun — the 'finished' meaning is already in -(으)ㄴ by itself: 보다 → 본 영화.

exampleSentence.note: 예쁘다 becomes 예쁜 before a noun.

exampleSentence.note: 크다 becomes 큰 before a noun.

exampleSentence.note: 작다 becomes 작은 before a noun.
새롭다 becomes 새로운; 새 is also common before nouns.

exampleSentence.en: I am fixing bad habits little by little.
exampleSentence.note: 나쁘다 becomes 나쁜 before a noun.

I will buy only the things I need.

extendedDialogue.setting: A customer identifies the exact bag in a shop by using adjective and verb modifiers.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: What kind of bag are you looking for?
lines.grammarNote: 어떤 asks for a description before the noun.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.ko: 어제 본 작은 가방을 찾고 있어요.
lines.romanization: eoje bon jageun gabangeul chatgo isseoyo.
lines.en: I am looking for the small bag I saw yesterday.
lines.grammarNote: 본 and 작은 both stand before 가방.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: It is a new model that customers ask for a lot.
lines.grammarNote: 찾는 is a verb modifier; 새로운 is an adjective modifier.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Is it a good bag to carry to work?
lines.grammarNote: 좋은 modifies 가방, and the phrase explains the purpose.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Yes, many necessary things fit inside too.

readingText.title: Finding the right bag
readingText.body: 민서는 출근할 때 들기 좋은 가방을 찾고 있었어요. 직원에게 어제 본 작은 가방이 아직 있는지 물어봤어요. 직원은 그 가방이 손님들이 많이 찾는 새로운 모델이라고 설명했어요. 안에는 필요한 물건이 꽤 많이 들어가고, 디자인도 예뻤어요. 민서는 바쁜 아침에도 들고 다니기 편한 가방이 필요했기 때문에 그 가방을 다시 한번 확인했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo was looking for a bag that would be good to carry to work. She asked whether the small bag she saw yesterday was still available. The staff explained that it was a new model customers often ask for, and Minseo checked it again because she needed a comfortable bag for busy mornings.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 어떤 가방을 찾고 있었어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 출근할 때 들기 좋은 가방을 찾고 있었어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 직원은 그 가방을 어떤 모델이라고 설명했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 손님들이 많이 찾는 새로운 모델이라고 설명했어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 민서는 왜 그 가방을 다시 확인했어요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 바쁜 아침에도 들고 다니기 편한 가방이 필요했기 때문이에요.

culturalNote.title: Descriptions make requests sound clear and polite
culturalNote.body: In shops, offices, and meet-up situations, Korean often avoids a long chain of short sentences by placing the description before the noun. 어제 봤어요. 작은 가방이에요. 그거 찾고 있어요 can become 어제 본 작은 가방을 찾고 있어요, which is clearer and more natural.
culturalNote.tip: When the listener has several possible items in mind, build one precise noun phrase: 조용한 카페, 제가 읽는 책, 어제 본 작은 가방.

inlineExercises.prompt: In a shop, which phrase identifies the item most clearly?
inlineExercises.explanation: Korean modifiers come before the noun they describe.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which phrase uses V-는 N correctly?
inlineExercises.explanation: 찾는 modifies 모델 with an action-based description.

inlineExercises.prompt: Change 조용하다 + 카페 into a noun phrase.
inlineExercises.explanation: 하다 adjectives become 한 before a noun.

inlineExercises.prompt: Change 읽다 + 책 into 'the book I am reading.'
inlineExercises.explanation: A present or habitual verb modifier uses 는.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the phrase: 제가 읽어요 책
inlineExercises.explanation: 읽어요 is a sentence ending; 읽는 modifies 책.
Adjective modifiers come before the noun.

inlineExercises.prompt: 작은 가방___ 찾고 있어요. (I am looking for a small bag.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 찾다 is an action, and 작은 가방 is what you are looking for, so it takes 을. 이 would make the bag the subject instead.
Adjectives describe nouns with -(으)ㄴ. 작다 becomes 작은 before 가방.
Present action modifiers use V-는 before the noun. 읽다 becomes 읽는 when it describes 책.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which phrase means “the bag I saw yesterday”?
inlineExercises.explanation: A completed action before a noun uses V-(으)ㄴ, so 보다 becomes 본. 가방 어제 봤어요 is a full sentence, not a noun phrase.

bullets: Adjective descriptions use A-ㄴ/은 N: 예쁜 가방, 작은 지갑, 조용한 카페.
Present or habitual action descriptions use V-는 N: 찾는 모델, 읽는 책, 사는 동네.
Completed action descriptions point to a noun already affected by an action: 어제 본 가방, 새로 들어온 물건.
Best check: if the word ends like a sentence, change it before placing it in front of a noun.

writingTask.prompt: Describe a lost item to staff at an information desk in 3 sentences: name the bag you're looking for, what's inside, and where you saw it.
writingTask.hint: Use A-(으)ㄴ N for adjectives (작은 가방), V-는 N for a current action (찾는 가방), and V-(으)ㄴ N for a finished one (어제 본 가방).
writingTask.model: 저는 작은 가방을 찾아요. 제가 찾는 가방은 까만색이에요. 어제 여기에서 본 가방이에요.
writingTask.modelEn: I'm looking for a small bag. The bag I'm looking for is black. It's the bag I saw here yesterday.

canDo: Put an adjective before a noun with A-(으)ㄴ N (작은 가방 · 예쁜 옷)
Describe a noun by a current or habitual action with V-는 N (찾는 가방)
Describe a noun by a finished action with V-(으)ㄴ N (어제 본 영화)
Pick out the exact person or thing I mean from several
